title: This Lion-Like Nebula Has Cosmic Dust for a Mane and a Dying Star for a Face
gist: The James Webb Space Telescope captured a new high-resolution infrared image of planetary nebula NGC 2392 — nicknamed the Lion Nebula by NASA — revealing its white-dwarf 'face' and dust-and-gas 'mane' in more detail than Hubble's 2000 photo.

themes.theme: The Lion Nebula's structure and imaging

insights.claim: Planetary nebula NGC 2392 resembles a lion's face, with its 'face' and darker 'nose' formed by the white dwarf remnant of the original star and an outer 'mane' produced from ionized gas and elongated strands of dust ejected from the star.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Describes the physical anatomy of a planetary nebula as the visible end-stage remnant of a dying sun-like star.
insights.quote: Its “face” and darker “nose” are the white dwarf remnants of the original star, an ultra-hot, sizzling core of everything that remains.
insights.locator: It's easy to see a lion's face

insights.claim: NGC 2392's 'Lion Nebula' nickname is now its official designation from NASA, and the James Webb Space Telescope has delivered a new high-resolution infrared image of it, complementing a Hubble Space Telescope photo taken in 2000.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Shows how successive space telescope generations (Hubble to Webb) are re-imaging the same known objects in new wavelengths to extract additional structural detail.
insights.quote: The Lion Nebula is actually now NGC 2392’s official NASA nickname, and the James Webb Telescope just delivered a new, high-resolution image of it in infrared vision, to go with a photo Hubble captured back in 2000.

insights.claim: Webb's infrared photography of NGC 2392 provides a clearer view than Hubble's of the dust and gas being blown away from the nebula's center, structures powered by radiation from the unstable, pulsating core star that can no longer sustain itself.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the practical advantage of infrared imaging over visible-light imaging for studying dust and gas dynamics in stellar remnants.
insights.quote: the infrared photography captured by the Webb Telescope provides a better look at the dust and gas that’s being blown away from the center of the shot
